beatOutlines.textOutline: Raju is thrilled watching Bharat Motors' chart at ₹420 today.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Sharma ji walks in and asks if he checked the bond market today.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Baffled, Raju asks why a stock trader should care about bonds or commodities.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Raju entered at the ₹420 peak, thinking the stock chart alone is enough.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Falling bonds pushed interest rates up, dragging Raju's stock from ₹420 to ₹375.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: John Murphy calls this Intermarket Analysis: no market trades in isolation.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Intermarket analysis tracks four global sectors, starting with currencies and the US Dollar.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: The second pillar is commodities like gold and oil, signaling inflation.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: The third pillar is bonds, whose prices move opposite to interest rates.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: The fourth pillar is stocks, guided by signals from the other three.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Normally, bond prices and stock prices move in the same direction.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Higher bond prices mean lower rates, boosting corporate profits and stocks.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Bonds usually turn before stocks, making bond drops an early warning.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Suppose the bond chart holds support at ₹105, keeping stocks calm.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: When bonds break their trendline to ₹94, rising rates threaten stocks soon.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: If stocks make new highs while bonds fall, the equity rally is losing footing.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Why do bonds fall? The answer lies in their tug-of-war with commodities.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Rising oil, copper, and grain prices spark inflation, the arch-enemy of bonds.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Higher rates crush bond prices, so commodities and bond prices move inversely.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: What drives commodities? The US Dollar, which moves inversely to raw materials.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Gold leads the commodity index: a falling Dollar lifts Gold first, then CRB.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Thus the chain locks in: a firm Dollar cools Gold and CRB, lifting bonds and stocks.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Watch out: normal rules flip when inflation gives way to deflation.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: In deflation, falling prices crush corporate profits, as seen in Japan after 1990.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: In deflation, bonds decouple from stocks: bonds rally while equities and commodities sink.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: During the 1998 deflationary wave, as stocks and commodities sank, bonds stood firm at ₹110.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Capital fled equities into safe bonds, propelling bond prices from ₹110 to ₹128.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Your turn. Read this intermarket setup and predict what lies ahead for stocks.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Think: Dollar down, Gold and commodities up, and bond prices falling.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Rising commodities and falling bonds warn of higher rates that will soon hurt stocks.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Raju now sees why buying Bharat Motors at ₹420 without checking bonds was a trap.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Sharma ji smiles: a smart chartist never trades in a silo; he watches all four markets.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Let us tie together the eight core principles of Intermarket Analysis.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Currencies, commodities, bonds, and stocks are linked; no market moves alone.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Bonds and stocks normally move together, with bonds leading equity turns.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Commodities move opposite to bonds, while the US Dollar moves opposite to commodities.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Gold leads commodities, and in deflation bonds rally while stocks and commodities fall.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Never read one chart in isolation: watch all four sectors to spot major turns early.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

summarySteps: Four markets interact: currencies, commodities, bonds, and stocks
No market trades in isolation; each sector influences the next
Bond prices and stocks normally move in the same direction
Bond turns usually lead stock market tops and bottoms
Commodities (CRB) and bond prices move in opposite directions
The US Dollar moves inversely to gold and commodity prices
Gold leads the broader commodity index at turning points
In deflation, bonds decouple and rally while stocks and commodities fall
bottomTakeaway: Discipline and grounded market understanding are essential for survival.
